name: Revocation of the Chiricahua Apache Reservation by Executive Order, October 30, 1876
citation: Executive Order of October 30, 1876, revoking the Executive Order of December 14, 1872
nations: Chiricahua Apache (Chokonen and related bands), today the Fort Sill Apache Tribe and Chiricahua people at Mescalero
promises: The Executive Order of December 14, 1872 set apart a Chiricahua reservation in southeastern Arizona, from Dragoon Springs along the Chiricahua and Peloncillo mountains to the Mexican border, within the Chiricahua homeland.
In the 1852 treaty Mangas Coloradas signed for the Chiricahua (10 Stat. 979), the United States undertook to designate and settle the Apaches' territorial boundaries.

breaches.what: The President revoked and cancelled the 1872 order setting apart the Chiricahua reservation. The Indian Claims Commission found this was part of a plan to remove all Chiricahua Apache from their homelands to the San Carlos Reservation, and that the Ojo Caliente reservation in New Mexico was abolished on August 25, 1877.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Executive Order of October 30, 1876, recorded in Royce, Indian Land Cessions (1899), and in Indian Claims Commission Finding 14(b), Fort Sill Apache Tribe v. United States, Dockets 30-A and 48-A (1968)

source.title: Fort Sill Apache Tribe et al. v. United States, Dockets 30-A and 48-A, Findings of Fact, June 28, 1968
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that no treaty of cession or agreement ever became operative with the Chiricahua, that their lands were taken by the United States without their consent or compensation, and that the taking was completed on September 4, 1886, when the Army forced the final surrender of Geronimo's band and removed almost all surviving Chiricahua as prisoners of war. It also found the United States never carried out its 1852 treaty obligation to designate Apache boundaries.

landTaken: The Chiricahua reservation of 1872 (Royce Area 600), and the wider Chiricahua aboriginal territory in southwestern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona found by the Indian Claims Commission (Finding 13(a), 1968), taken as of September 4, 1886.
compensation: $15,967,300 for the aboriginal lands (Dockets 30-A and 48-A) and $521,796 (Dockets 30 and 48), by final judgment on a stipulated settlement, August 25, 1971.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe tells its history as that of Chiricahua survivors whose homeland spanned eastern Arizona and western New Mexico, who were held as prisoners of war in Florida, Alabama and Oklahoma until 1914, of whom about a third kept demanding the lands they had been promised, and who have since regained small holdings in their home territory, including a New Mexico reservation proclaimed in 2011.

openQuestions: The 1872 reservation followed General O. O. Howard's agreement with Cochise; that agreement's terms were not located in a primary source in this pass.

The Treaty with the Apaches of July 1, 1852 (10 Stat. 979) is not in the Royce queue because it ceded no land; the Commission's finding that its boundary obligation was never carried out could support an extra-<slug> file.
The Chiricahua's 27 years as prisoners of war (Florida, Alabama, Fort Sill) and the 1913 division between Fort Sill and Mescalero were not researched for findings.
treaties.json lists no present-day tribes for this cession; the Fort Sill Apache Tribe of Oklahoma is the plaintiff successor in the Commission's case.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1971 final judgment was entered on the parties' stipulation, so it is a settlement and its kind was changed from claims-commission to litigation; the 1968 findings of a taking without consent or compensation remain the claims-commission finding. The open question saying the Tribe's own account was not sought was dropped because nationVoice now holds it.

plain.promised: An 1872 presidential order set apart a Chiricahua reservation in southeastern Arizona, within the Chiricahua homeland. In an 1852 treaty the United States undertook to designate and settle the Apaches' boundaries.
plain.happened: The President revoked the reservation in 1876. The Indian Claims Commission found in 1968 that Chiricahua lands were taken without consent or compensation, completed in 1886 when the Army removed almost all surviving Chiricahua as prisoners of war.
plain.today: A stipulated settlement in 1971 gave final judgments of $15,967,300 and $521,796. The record was not researched past that judgment.
